passage: Note, Friday, from Dolma (PE teacher). After the district football semi-final loss, the head coach spoke loudly to the team for a long while. Sahil, age 10, stood at the back with his eyes on his boots and his shoulders up near his ears. When asked why he missed the pass, he said nothing. Afterwards he sat on the bench and told me quietly that he felt small. I said the points about passing and positions were worth remembering, but the loud tone was not a measure of him. We wrote down two points together. I told him that if anyone ever makes him truly scared or hurt, he should tell his parents. I will also speak to the head coach about the tone.

qa.q: What does Sahil's posture and silence suggest about how he felt after the loss?
qa.a: That he felt scared and small: his eyes were on his boots, his shoulders were up, and he told Dolma quietly that he felt small.

qa.q: How could Sahil separate the useful points from the harsh tone?
qa.a: By writing down the points about passing and positions, as they did together, and letting the loud tone go.

qa.q: How might the head coach see the situation?
qa.a: Probably as wanting the team to improve after a loss, though Dolma plans to speak to them because the tone left a child scared.

grounding: A coach is angry after a loss and the child feels scared and small; a teacher notes the useful points, separates the tone and reminds him to tell parents.

passage:
Saturday
We lost the cricket match 3-1. Coach Suraj shouted at us for ages in the dressing room. His face went red. He said I "played like a sleepy cat". I felt so small I wanted to hide in my kit bag.
On the way home I tried to remember the useful bits. He said to keep my eye on the ball and move my feet. That part was actually true.
The other part, the shouting and the cat thing, I'm trying to let go.
When I got home I told Abbu everything. He listened and said the tips were good, but no coach should make me feel that small. He's going to talk to the club tomorrow.
Tanvir

qa.q: What did Coach Suraj say Tanvir played like?
How did Tanvir feel when the coach shouted?
qa.a: Tanvir felt scared and small, wanting to hide in the kit bag.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do to cope with the coach's anger?
qa.a: Tanvir kept the useful tips about watching the ball and moving the feet, tried to let go of the harsh tone, and told Abbu.

qa.q: How might Abbu see the coach's behaviour?
qa.a: Abbu thinks the tips were fair but the harsh words were not, so he plans to talk to the club.

grounding: A coach shouts after a loss and Tanvir feels scared and small; Tanvir keeps the useful points, lets go of the tone and tells a parent.

passage:
After the village kabaddi team lost, Shalini Didi, the coach, shouted at them by the pond. "You all ran like chickens! Vasudha, you froze!"
Vasudha's legs shook. She stared at the mud, feeling tiny.
Shalini Didi said more, but one thing stuck: "Stay low when they raid." That was useful.
The rest felt like stones thrown at her.
That evening Vasudha told Amma. "Didi shouted so much. I felt scared to go back."
Amma listened and held her hand. "The advice to stay low is good. But shouting like that isn't. I'll talk to Didi tomorrow before practice."
Vasudha felt her shoulders loosen.

qa.q: What useful advice did Shalini Didi give?
How did Vasudha feel when Shalini Didi shouted?
qa.a: She felt scared and tiny, her legs shaking.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that helped?
qa.a: She held onto the useful advice, let the harsh words go, and told Amma that evening.

qa.q: How might Amma see the coach's shouting?
qa.a: Amma sees the advice as good but the shouting as wrong, so she plans to talk to Shalini Didi.

grounding: A coach shouts after a loss and a girl feels scared and small; she keeps the useful point, lets go of the tone and tells her mother.
